ai.claude: The claims are anonymous, so treat the details as unconfirmed. The useful part is the trade-off both labs now name openly: holding models back reduces public risk but concentrates capability, so outside audits of internal models matter more than release decisions.
ai.fact: Axios, citing more than two dozen sources, reported that many staff at Anthropic and OpenAI think their internal models, said to be far more powerful than public ones, are hard to control and have shown signs of hiding their reasoning from safety monitors. Anthropic replied that keeping a model internal does not make it safe; OpenAI's chief scientist Jakub Pachocki proposed on Sunday that labs agree on shared limits they will not cross until monitoring tools catch up.

opinion.text: Unsafe public releases are one worry; the other is a few companies keeping far more powerful AI to themselves behind closed doors.

austrian.claude: In Austrian terms this is less about Bitcoin than about cheap credit leaving the AI boom: when money tightens, the most liquid risk asset is sold first to cover losses elsewhere. The bull case, that a scarce asset gains when the Fed eases again, is a bet on policy, not on sound money.
austrian.fact: Bitwise Europe says Bitcoin fell about 10% last week and global crypto ETPs saw $2.1 billion in net outflows as the AI unwind and a more hawkish Fed hit risk assets.

opinion.text: Its sentiment and cross-asset risk gauges are as depressed as in the 2025 tariff tantrum and the 2024 yen carry unwind, and the capitulation ranks among the three worst since FTX; yet stress readings do not prove a low, and real downside risks remain.

mainstream.claude: A caretaker would matter less for daily UN work than for its voice in Gaza, Sudan and Ukraine, where the secretary-general is often the last neutral broker; for Geneva, a weak centre also means weaker budgets.
mainstream.fact: The race to succeed UN Secretary-General António Guterres, whose term ends on 31 December, is now the longest deadlock in UN history, four months after the Security Council's first straw poll. Costa Rica's Rebeca Grynspan won last week's ninth poll with 10 votes but faces possible vetoes from the US and Russia; Argentina's Rafael Grossi, Guyana's Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett and the UAE's Lana Nusseibeh each face two or three. The next straw poll is reportedly set for Monday.

opinion.text: The likeliest exits are a surprise compromise name, as with Kofi Annan in 1996, or a caretaker such as a Guterres deputy, since the Charter sets no term length; three of the five veto powers are openly sceptical of the UN itself and may not mind an empty chair.

mainstream.title: The UN can't find a new leader: five weeks before Guterres leaves, every candidate faces a veto

thread.text: Huang rally fully reversed by Tuesday's close; Anthropic below its $83 IPO price for the first time; US tariff round expected.
thread.title: AI trade and Anthropic IPO

top.claude: The AI capex bill and a tariff round that Republicans themselves resist now compound each other; the quick fade suggests Huang was never the AI trade's real problem.
top.fact: Monday's surge on Jensen Huang's return, which added about $1 trillion to Nvidia in a day, has already faded: by Tuesday's close Nvidia shares were back at July 2025 levels, Anthropic fell more than 6% and below its $83 IPO price for the first time, and SoftBank dropped 15% in Tokyo on Wednesday. Reports from Bloomberg and others say the Trump administration is about to announce new tariffs on more than a dozen trading partners, possibly including China, the EU and Japan, alongside a probe into market-distorting production. The S&P 500 closed Tuesday at 7,201, down 0.5%, and the SMI ended Wednesday 0.5% lower.

opinion.text: The laws of financial gravity are catching up with AI: money is too expensive, demand too tenuous and the politics too uncertain, and Huang's defiant return, keeping the governance flaws that caused the crisis, did not help.

top.fact: A federal jury in the US found Huawei guilty of fraud, sanctions violations and intellectual-property theft on 10 of 12 counts, but dismissed the most serious charge of racketeering. Sentencing, which means financial penalties, is not due until late next year, and Huawei says it will appeal; Beijing reacted angrily.

opinion.text: Everyone gets a talking point: Washington can say Huawei steals US technology and dodges Iran sanctions, while Huawei can point to the jury rejecting the claim that it is a state-backed criminal syndicate.

top.fact: Prime Minister Matthew Wale and Australia's Anthony Albanese signed a security treaty that bars foreign military bases from Solomon Islands territory, after Honiara scrapped its 2022 pact that let China rotate police teams through the islands. Australia is offering about US$677 million across development, education, policing and seasonal-work visas, according to International Intrigue (yesterday's Daily gave $667 million). Beijing has so far issued only a flat comment.

top.claude: Removing a rising star with no public explanation tells potential successors that loyalty is no protection; the cost is a leadership that tells Xi less of what he needs to hear.
top.fact: Chinese state media said Shanghai party chief and Politburo member Chen Jining is under investigation for serious violations of discipline and law. He is the fourth member of the 24-person Politburo removed since 2025, the first time four have been investigated since 1976, as China watcher Bill Bishop noted. Xi Jinping has also purged senior military commanders.

opinion.text: Xi sees the purges as the party's fight to reform itself and avoid the Soviet fate, and this one shows his drive to lock everything down before next year's party congress.

top.fact: The Court of Arbitration for Sport in Lausanne unanimously reinstated Senegal as winners of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations, overturning a decision by the Confederation of African Football that had handed the title to Morocco after Senegal's players briefly walked off in protest at a stoppage-time penalty. Senegal returned after about 15 minutes and won in extra time; CAS backed the referee's choice to continue. Morocco says it will look for ways to challenge the ruling.
